name: Freya Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and your answers are confidential. What does a regular day on the lines involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the live-line crew, working on energized wires from insulated bucket trucks so customers can keep power. My two-year technical diploma taught the theory; a wet glove or a cracked insulator teaches you to slow down. I like the concentration of a clean repair.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What has changed in your day lately?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use an AI tool every morning to sort drone photos, then check the marks with my own eyes. My partner Ingrid runs a local bakery, and our grown children have their own homes. The long drive between jobs wears me out more than the new software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the live-line team that a small time saving is still a saving if the drone list is checked. My daily AI tool may be unglamorous, but I like getting the inspection photos sorted before we leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Ingrid and I own our home and have more than six months saved. My pay is high for this work, and the nearby utilities would have room for someone with live-line skills, so a plateau does not threaten our plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the live-line rota and use the same drone-image sorter every morning. I would also keep setting aside wages at our present rate; I would not buy a new robotic arm just to chase a small gain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even amused. I would rather have an honest little tool than a big promise nobody can test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you check after the drone sorter runs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cracked insulators, hot joints and shadows that look like damage. A false mark can send a crew miles out of its way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you bored if it stays small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But I still get to solve hard line faults, and there is enough work to take me to the retirement date Ingrid and I have discussed.

say: I would call my existing **drone sorter** useful even if AI improves little else.
I would tell the crew that **photo marks** still need a lineworker’s eyes.
think: Our **paid home**, higher wages and strong savings make the plateau secure for Ingrid and me.
I would miss the chance to test a **better field tool**, though not the income.
do: Keep the **live-line rota** and check daily drone marks against the images.
Continue the existing **wage savings** amount without buying a new arm.
feel: **Calm**, with mild disappointment that the tool stays small.
S0.quote: A false mark can send a crew miles out of its way.
fieldNote: Her regular AI use is already part of **normal inspection**, so no new learning is implied.
The household has several buffers and **plenty of nearby jobs**, supporting her calm assessment.

steps.text: Keep live-line shifts and verify the existing drone sorter marks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our crew that buying and booking may be quicker, but I want the lineworkers reviewing every repair priority. I would bring a checklist to the co-op safety circle, where members and crews meet. The ranking can be fast and still send a truck down a closed road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office may shrink while the live-line trucks keep running. My own wage looks safe, and Ingrid still has her own work, but the new starters could lose the people who teach them the route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would join the next safety circle with a checklist for dispatch errors. Once the co-op offers a new AI fault-ranking screen, I would learn its settings and compare its top ten calls with our crew notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the apprentices, curious about the screen. My own household is not short of money in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be on the checklist?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The feeder number, who verified the isolation, and whether the road is passable. If the ranking hides any of those, I would ask the circle to hold it back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is Ingrid’s wage at risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cannot know every job affected, but Ingrid runs a small local bakery and I have not heard anything suggesting its orders would fall here. I am judging our household from what we actually know.

say: I would ask **lineworkers** to review AI repair priorities before crews are dispatched.
I would take a **three-point checklist** to the co-op safety circle.
think: My **live-line wage** looks secure, although the office may have fewer posts.
I worry new starters could lose **human mentors** during a broad shift in planning.
do: Join the **co-op safety circle** with dispatch checks for feeder, isolation and road access.
Learn the new **AI fault-ranking settings** when offered and compare ten calls with crew notes.
feel: **Uneasy** for apprentices, while my own household income appears sound.
S1.quote: The ranking can be fast and still send a truck down a closed road.
fieldNote: Her co-op participation is actual **group action** with a defined, practical safety proposal for dispatch.
She distinguishes new fault-ranking skills from her **existing drone sorter** work.

steps.text: Join the co-op safety circle with three dispatch checks
Learn new AI fault-ranking settings when offered and compare ten crew calls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the thinking AI in 2028 can mark a bad insulator, but a person still takes the bucket truck up. When capable robots arrive around 2031, I want live-line trials that show every stop and mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I aim to leave regular line work before the robot date if our health and accounts hold, and Ingrid’s bakery income is separate. I could still take a paid trial role if it exists, but I am not counting on a job that has not been offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the co-op for a paid field trial and learn the new robot-control interface if a funded place opens. I would stay on my present shifts while they are offered and review our retirement date with Ingrid before accepting any trial role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the speed, not frightened for our bills. The young crew have fewer years to find their footing than I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for the controls course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could afford one, but I would only do it as part of a real paid field role with a vacancy. I am not collecting certificates for a job that does not exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would end a trial immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A missing isolation reading or a robot moving when the bucket operator has called stop. I want the stop command tested before any live conductor is touched.

say: I would demand **live-line trials** showing stops and errors before 2031 robots work near energized conductors.
I would ask the **co-op** for paid crew involvement in those trials.
think: I expect to finish regular field work before **2031** if our accounts and health hold.
A paid **trial vacancy** could interest me, but it is not yet an income plan.
do: Learn the new **robot-control interface** only if a funded paid field vacancy opens.
Keep **present live-line shifts** while offered and review retirement timing with Ingrid.
feel: **Uneasy** about the short lead time, while household money remains secure.
S2.quote: I am not collecting certificates for a job that does not exist.
fieldNote: The training depends on a **funded vacancy**, not mere interest in new machines.
Her expected retirement before the robot phase is conditional on **health and accounts**, without an early-exit decision.

steps.text: Learn robot controls only if a funded paid field vacancy opens
Keep live-line shifts while offered and review retirement timing with Ingrid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team that five years is enough to test a repair robot through wet mornings and awkward pole angles. A polished demonstration on dry ground would not persuade me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2031 will make the inspection list smarter, which I can verify. Robots reach hands-on work around 2034, likely after I have left regular field shifts if Ingrid and I keep to our plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would continue the live-line rota next year and volunteer for a paid two-week control trial if the co-op runs one. I would keep a log of missed stop commands and give it to the safety circle before any wider use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my own wage. Five years is enough to measure a machine properly, if people actually listen to the measurements.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the co-op offers no paid trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current job and ask for the test results when they exist. I would not leave a well paid crew lead role for an unpaid demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who sees the log first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bucket operator and the safety circle together. A control failure belongs in the open, not in my private notebook.

say: I would insist on **wet-weather trials** before 2034 repair robots get live-line work.
I would share a **stop-command log** with the crew and co-op safety circle.
think: My own **field shifts** likely finish before 2034 if our plan holds.
The **2031 inspection system** is manageable because I already verify AI image marks daily.
do: Keep leading **live-line shifts** during the first year.
Run a **paid two-week control trial** if offered and log missed stop commands for the safety circle.
feel: **Calm** about my pay, determined to make test failures visible.
S3.quote: A control failure belongs in the open, not in my private notebook.
fieldNote: She is willing to trial equipment only in a **paid role** that the co-op actually offers.
The five-year lead lets her create **usable evidence** before robots reach field repairs.

steps.text: Keep leading live-line shifts during the first year
Run a paid two-week robot-control trial if offered and log failed stops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our co-op that ten years is enough to train a full generation of live-line workers. Thinking AI in 2036 and robots around 2039 should arrive with a clear right to stop unsafe work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect to be retired from regular line work before 2036 if our savings and health stay on track. I may still volunteer my experience in a paid training role if an actual vacancy opens, but I will not assume one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now in 2026, I would keep using the drone-image sorter and stay on my crew. At the next co-op safety circle I would propose a stop-work rule for robotic repairs, with apprentices included in the discussion. In the first year after 2036 I expect to be retired if our plan holds; if still employed, I would retain those checks and stop-work rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm for our household and energized about the younger workers. A decade can be used well if the crew has a say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire earlier because of this card?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The timetable is longer than the one Ingrid and I are already discussing, and our decision depends on health and savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the stop-work rule say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Any qualified lineworker on site may stop a robot repair when the isolation record or movement looks wrong. A robot operator must not have to ask the office before stopping an unsafe live-line repair.

say: I would seek a **stop-work rule** before 2039 robots reach energized lines.
I would invite **apprentices** to the co-op safety circle discussion.
think: I expect to retire from field work before **2036** if savings and health permit.
A future paid **training vacancy** is possible, but I cannot count it as an offer.
do: **Keep** live-line shifts and drone-image checks now; continue after 2036 only if still employed.
Propose a **robot stop-work rule** at the next co-op safety circle with apprentices present.
feel: **Calm** about our household and purposeful about younger workers’ safety.
S4.quote: A robot operator must not have to ask the office before stopping an unsafe live-line repair.
fieldNote: She preserves the existing retirement plan and does not label a **possible teaching role** as secured work.
The group action is a concrete **co-op rule proposal** that includes apprentices.

steps.text: Keep live-line shifts and drone checks now and after 2036 only if still employed
Propose robot stop-work rule with apprentices at the next co-op safety circle

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 is the hardest for the younger live-line crew, because robots could reach field work by 2031 before they have much practice. Paid trials with clear stop rules and a real training vacancy would help; Ingrid and I have enough savings to protect our own plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who can press stop when a repair robot moves near a live conductor. A stop button is only useful if the worker is allowed to use it.

headlineQuote: A stop button is only useful if the worker is allowed to use it.
portrait: **Freya**, 58, leads live-line repairs with a technical diploma, higher pay, strong savings and many nearby utility jobs.
She uses **AI daily** for drone inspections and is eager to learn controls only in a real funded role.
Her co-op **safety-circle work** focuses on visible trial failures, apprentices and a right to stop robotic repairs.
She expects to retire before robots reach field work if household **health and accounts** hold, leaving younger crews as her main concern.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives younger live-line workers little practice time before capable robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **field trials**, stop rules and a real training vacancy would help the younger crew.
